newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU moves closer to fining TACA shipping companies.
newsitem.headline: EU moves closer to fining TACA shipping companies.

text.p: The European Commission said on Thursday it had lifted the immunity to fines of 17 shipping companies in the Trans-Atlantic Conference Agreement (TACA), moving a step closer to penalising them for anti-competitive behaviour.

The decision, which had been expected for almost two years, marks the Commission's determination to get changes to TACA which involves in particular Sea-Land Service of the United States, Atlantic Container Line AB, Hapag-Lloyd AG of Germany and Neptune Orient Lines Ltd of Singapore.
TACA is a liner conference which, according to the Commission, controls more than 60 percent of the regular sea container transport between Europe and North America.
The Commission banned an earlier version called the Trans-Atlantic Agreement in October 1994 for fixing the rate of inland transport to and from ports, but the practice has not been abolished.
"The Commission decided today to adopt a decision lifting the immunity from fines benefiting the TACA parties...in respect of inland rate fixing," it said in a statement.

But the actual decision on whether to fine the companies, which under EU rules could amount to as much as 10 percent of the companies' annual turnover in the Union, would not be taken for at least another six months, a Commission official told Reuters.

In a separate case, the Commission announced it had been formally notified of the merger of the container shipping interests of Britain's P&O Co and Nedlloyd Groep whose subsidiaries P&O Containers Ltd and Nedlloyd Lijnen BV are also TACA members.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has declined to say whether he will use this case as leverage for obtaining changes to the TACA agreement. But Brussels-based lawyers say this is unlikely.
EU legislation on liner conferences permits price fixing only for sea, and not land transport.
TACA members had been immune from fines because they submitted the TAA, then the TACA agreement for clearance under EU competition rules.
Thursday's decision did not apply to South Korea's Hyundai Merchant Marine Co Ltd which joined TACA recently, the Commission said.

The European Court of Justice is set to have the final word in the heated four-year battle. TACA members have already said they will appeal any fines in the European court. They won a previous a battle in March 1995, when the European Court of First Instance, the EU's lower court, ordered the suspension of the Commission's TAA decision.
The court has still to rule on the substance of the case.

The Court of Justice itself is expected to rule next year on a case referred by a British court on whether inland rate fixing is covered by the EU legislation on liner conferences. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
